summary:
The Ocean's Hidden Response is an interactive scientific website developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026's "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge.

The project investigates historical surface chlorophyll-a and sea surface temperature observations in two Pacific regions. Visitors can explore monthly measurements, examine regional trends, inspect statistical uncertainty, and download data and methods to reproduce the findings.

Using observations from January 2013 through December 2025, the analysis found estimated chlorophyll-a declines of 16.31% and 17.76% per decade in the Eastern Equatorial Pacific and Northwestern Tropical Pacific, respectively. However, the direct comparison did not establish a statistically significant difference between their relative trends.

The website helps students, educators, and scientific reviewers investigate historical ocean changes while accounting for seasonality, missing observations, and statistical uncertainty.
details:
Introduction

The Ocean's Hidden Response is a publicly accessible scientific web application that allows users to investigate historical ocean changes using satellite-derived Earth observation data.

Problem and objective

Satellite observations reveal changes in ocean conditions, but interpreting long-term trends requires accounting for seasonal cycles, missing measurements, and statistical uncertainty.

Our project investigates how surface chlorophyll-a changed in two predefined Pacific regions and whether their relative trends differed. Sea surface temperature provides an additional Earth-system variable for exploration.

Study regions and observations

The investigation covers:

  • Eastern Equatorial Pacific (EEP): 120°W to 90°W, 5°S to 5°N.
  • Northwestern Tropical Pacific (NWP): 125°E to 150°E, 2°N to 10°N.

The reference analysis covers January 2013 through December 2025, representing 156 calendar months. Each primary reference trend fit includes 154 eligible monthly observations.

The primary chlorophyll-a record comes from NOAA Suomi-NPP VIIRS. Sea surface temperature is derived from NASA JPL MUR through NOAA monthly composites. A separate NASA MODIS Aqua January 2013 record was processed for limited source verification.

How the application works

Visitors can select chlorophyll-a or sea surface temperature, choose either region or both, and explore monthly observations within selected date windows.

Interactive charts display historical measurements, estimated rates of change, and confidence intervals. The website also provides a Pacific geographic locator, explanations of the scientific methods, information about missing observations, and data-source attribution.

Users can share selected investigations through URL parameters and download observations and reproducibility materials.

Scientific methodology

The Python processing pipeline aggregates satellite observations within the predefined regions. Chlorophyll-a uses a cosine-latitude area-weighted geometric mean, while temperature uses an area-weighted arithmetic mean.

Long-term changes are estimated using regression models with calendar-time trends and monthly seasonal effects. Chlorophyll-a is analyzed on a logarithmic scale and reported as a relative percentage change per decade. Temperature trends are reported in degrees Celsius per decade.

Approximate statistical uncertainty is estimated using heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation-consistent covariance methods. A paired analysis of aligned regional log-chlorophyll observations directly evaluates the relative regional trend difference.

Scientific findings

For January 2013 through December 2025:

  • EEP chlorophyll-a trend: -16.31% per decade, with an approximate 95% confidence interval of -23.66% to -8.25%.
  • NWP chlorophyll-a trend: -17.76% per decade, with an approximate 95% confidence interval of -26.26% to -8.29%.
  • Direct relative trend comparison: +1.77% per decade, with an approximate 95% confidence interval of -12.73% to +18.67% and p = 0.822.

Both individual chlorophyll-a trend estimates were negative, and their approximate confidence intervals excluded zero. However, the direct comparison did not establish a statistically significant difference between their relative trends.

Technical implementation and reproducibility

The application uses HTML, CSS, and modular JavaScript. Python handles scientific data processing and statistical analysis. Node.js, GitHub Actions, and Playwright support development, automated verification, and browser testing.

The application is hosted publicly using GitHub Pages and operates on prepared historical observations without requiring a user account or live satellite-data access.

The repository includes source code, scientific methods, processed observations, reference results, and downloadable reproduction materials.

Source code:

https://github.com/seezel/ocean-hidden-response

Public application:

https://seezel.github.io/ocean-hidden-response/

Limitations and future work

The findings describe two predefined regions and selected historical satellite products. The observational analysis cannot establish the causes of chlorophyll-a changes or predict future ocean conditions.

Potential future work includes validating additional ocean regions, comparing independent satellite products, and conducting further accessibility testing.

The project provides an accessible way for students, educators, and scientific reviewers to examine ocean observations while considering seasonal variation, missing data, and statistical uncertainty.
